source: https://elibrary.maff.gov.kh/assets/files/books/a4cc69c087a47633f2aec73f8c462b801626315648.pdf (Khmer translation of an IRRI rice growth/physiology primer, credited to Dr. B.S. Vergara)
text: Weeds reduce rice yield in every season, not just under poor conditions, by competing directly with the rice plant for light, nutrients, and water. A weedy field produces visibly fewer and smaller filled grain bags at harvest than a weed-free field planted the same way. Fertilizer makes this worse rather than better if weeds are not controlled: as more fertilizer is applied to a weedy field, the weeds absorb an increasing share of it alongside the rice, so a farmer who fertilizes heavily without weeding is partly just feeding the weeds. Cambodian rice-field weeds are grouped into three practical categories based on leaf shape, leaf vein pattern, and stem cross-section: grasses (ស្មៅព្រៃក្រាមីនេ) have narrow, parallel-veined leaves and round or hollow stems -- a common example is barnyard grass, Echinochloa crus-galli (ស្មៅជើងកា); sedges (ស្មៅព្រៃស៊ីពែរ៉ាសេ) have narrow leaves but triangular stems -- a common example is Cyperus iria (កកព្រុង); and broadleaf weeds (ស្មៅព្រៃស្លឹកធំ) have wider leaves with branching veins and round or square stems -- a common example is Monochoria vaginalis (ត្រកួន, also eaten as a vegetable but a competitive weed in rice). Because young grass weeds can look very similar to young rice seedlings, one reliable field trick is to check the leaf collar where the leaf blade meets the stem: true rice has both a ligule (a small membranous flap, អណ្ដាតសួប) and an auricle (a pair of small claw-like extensions, ព្រុយ) at this junction, while many grassy weeds lack one or both of these structures, letting a farmer distinguish rice from weedy grass even before either one flowers. Timing matters more than total weeding effort: yield data in the source shows that yield loss becomes severe once a field is left unweeded for more than about 30 days after transplanting/establishment, so the first 30 days is the critical weed-free period, and weeding should begin within that window rather than being delayed until weeds are already well established.
